extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy and constitutional theory
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and interpretation of classical accounts (Polybius, Plato, Roman practice) about forms of government, their virtues, vices, and institutional arrangements. The page discusses causes of generation/corruption of governments and prescriptions for constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound government (mixture of forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The best form of government is not simple, but compounded” — a constitution tempered with monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polybius and Valerius argue that mixing monarchical, aristocratic, and democratic elements yields the most perfect form: each part restrains the excesses of the others. Examples/claims: the Roman constitution (as an example of mixed government) and England as an instance of an equal mixture. Avoid purely simple forms because each tends to its own vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and balances between orders
rubrics_metrics.description: The different orders (consuls, senate, people) have powers “to oppose, assist, and balance each other, as occasion may require.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional design should ensure that branches can check one another so no branch 'swell beyond its bounds.' The union of orders adapted to contingencies produces strength and prevents omission or delay in public business (e.g., in wartime acting in concert).

rubrics_metrics.name: People's share and negative (popular oversight and accountability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Granting the people a share in government preserves liberty and power; the people have the power of distributing honours and punishments and can confirm or reject measures of other branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valerius' speech: allow the people to choose annual magistrates, to confirm/repeal laws, declare war and make peace, and try offenders accused of crimes against the state. Popular negatives/tribunes serve as checks against senatorial or executive abuse; public trials and ratification are accountability mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers / executive-legislative control
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive was 'never sufficiently separated from the legislative' and lacked defined controls to interpose between people and senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design should clearly define inter-branch powers so the executive can be constrained and cannot dominate legislation. The text criticizes insufficiently defined mutual controls and urges clearer limits so no branch can act without checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited terms and plural magistrates to avoid tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistracies should be limited in duration (e.g., consuls for a year) and plural (multiple consuls) to prevent monarchical/tyrannical concentration of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short terms and collegial magistracies (and councils of elders/senators to watch them) are recommended safeguards. The author argues that with adequate representation of the people, appointment of dictators becomes unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and oversight of generals (civil control of the military)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generals stand in need of the people and senate; they must give an account of their conduct after command and cannot celebrate triumphs without senate consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military commanders should depend on civil authorities for supplies, pay, and honors; civil consent (senate/people) for triumphs and settlements prevents military autonomy and usurpation—e.g., senate can appoint successors or continue command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and cultivation of civic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is 'the grand point to be attended to' to produce guardians/rulers with the virtues (fortitude, temperance, wisdom, justice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's model: institutionalized education shapes citizens and rulers so the constitution can produce and sustain virtue; promotion across classes (raising worthy to guardian rank) supports meritocratic stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency of simple forms to degenerate (rotation of governments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every simple form of government has a natural vice and will degenerate: monarchy→tyranny, aristocracy→oligarchy, democracy→rage and violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical/cyclical diagnosis: because each simple form carries an internal tendency to corruption, constitutions should be designed (via mixture, education, checks) to prevent or slow such degeneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful selection and promotion of guardians/rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistakes in choosing guardians and in rewarding/promoting merit cause discord (e.g., mixing 'iron' and 'bronze' geniuses with gold/silver).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional procedures for selection and promotion must accurately identify and advance genuine merit; errors in personnel selection can fracture the polity and lead to sedition and faction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate institutional representation for wealthy elites
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the rich and proud 'into one group, in a separate assembly' to tie their hands and make them a check on representatives and the executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolating wealthy interests into a distinct chamber/assembly channels their abilities and virtues while preventing them from dominating popular elections or corrupting representatives; this reduces the risk of a natural aristocracy capturing general government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of inspectors and guards to enforce laws and deter ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: Appoint 'many inspectors, and many guards over the insolent and the ambitious' so transgressions of the laws are formidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical enforcement mechanisms—inspectors, oversight bodies, and public accountability—are necessary to deter and punish those who would corrupt or subvert the constitution; increasing the difficulty of transgression improves discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of public finances as central power
rubrics_metrics.description: The senate (or an assembly) having command of public money—conduct of receipts and disbursements—is a principal branch of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Financial control (who can issue or disburse funds) is an essential lever of authority; restricting unilateral financial action (e.g., consuls cannot issue money without senate decree) constrains executive and military overreach.
